subject: Clarify: storage and deletion windows for user queries vs model responses
messages:
From: Alex Harris <alex.harris@finbridge.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-04-10T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Questions re: what Redwood stores by default (requests vs outputs)

Marissa / team,

Thanks for the quick onboarding last week — our security and procurement teams have a few follow-ups on default storage behavior before we can sign the SOW. Wanted to confirm a few concrete items so I can pass them along to InfoSec: 

- By default, what does Redwood retain from a single request/response cycle? Do you keep the raw user prompt (our users' input) and the model-generated text (the output) both?
- For streaming responses (clients that stream token-by-token), are intermediate fragments persisted anywhere or only the final assembled response?
- How is KV cache / session state handled? If a session is idle, does any cached context persist beyond the immediate worker memory?
- What are the deletion timelines and how do you evidence deletion for us if we need proof? For example: tombstones, purge job run cadence, backups, and whether there's a secondary retention in snapshots/backups.
- Residency: for our EU users we must ensure data (requests) remain in EU-hosted storage — what guarantees can you give by default, and what changes under Dedicated/Private?

I attached the current SOW excerpt for context. If easier, we can schedule a short call — but a short written summary that I can hand to our legal team would be ideal.

Appreciate it,
Alex
Alex Harris
Security Lead, FinBridge
alex.harris@finbridge.com
Attachment: Finbridge_SOW.pdf
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
To: Alex Harris <alex.harris@finbridge.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-04-10T12:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Questions re: what Redwood stores by default (requests vs outputs)

Alex — thanks for the clear list. I wanted to give a concise, customer-facing summary first; Kimberly (security/ops) and Ben (sales/contract) are looped for technical and contractual detail. High-level answers below:

- Default capture: by default our Hosted API stores the incoming request (the raw prompt/text you send) and the final model response. These artifacts are kept to support debugging, abuse detection, quality monitoring, and to provide customers with audit evidence when requested.

- Streaming behavior: intermediate streaming fragments are not persistently stored as separate artifacts. We assemble the streamed tokens into the final response during the request session; only the final assembled response is eligible for retention.

- KV cache / session state: KV cache is maintained in-memory for the lifetime of the serving session and is not persisted as a durable artifact by default. It may survive briefly on the node until eviction but is not indexed in our long-term stores unless customer chooses to persist session traces.

- Deletion timelines & evidence: our standard Hosted retention window is 45 days for stored requests+final responses. Deletion is a two-step process: marking/tombstoning followed by background purge jobs. Tombstone -> purge typically completes within 72 hours; backups/snapshots may retain encrypted records for an additional 30 days for disaster recovery, after which backup retention expires and records are truncated. For customers who require formal proof, we provide a deletion certificate (signed timestamp + object ids) and a short runbook summary.

- Residency: by default data is stored in the region corresponding to the request routing (US or EU). For strict EU-only residency we recommend Redwood Dedicated or Redwood Private where you can pin storage to customer VPC/region; we also support region-limited contracts and Data Processing Addendums (DPAs) on enterprise plans.

Next steps: 
1) Kimberly, can you expand on the technical purge/backup lifecycle and confirm logs we can provide as evidence?
2) Alex, if FinBridge needs SCC or an amended DPA clause, Ben and I can follow up with a redline.

Happy to hop on a 30m call if that speeds things up.

—
Marissa Cole
Head of Customer Success, Redwood Inference
marissa@redwood.com
Redwood Inference — https://redwood.com
From: Kimberly Park <kimberly@redwood.com>
To: Alex Harris <alex.harris@finbridge.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-04-12T08:30:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Questions re: what Redwood stores by default (requests vs outputs) — technical detail

On Apr 10, 2028, at 12:05 PM, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com> wrote:
> Alex — thanks for the clear list. I wanted to give a concise, customer-facing summary first; Kimberly (security/ops) and Ben (sales/contract) are looped for technical and contractual detail. High-level answers below:

Quick technical addendum and precise mechanics to support the summary above: 

- What we persist: the request payload (HTTP body) and the final generated output are written to our object store as JSON artifacts (indexed by request id). Metadata (timestamps, model version, route id, region) is stored in our metadata db. We consider the request text and final answer "stored artifacts" by default.

- Streaming fragments: token-level fragments flow through an in-memory streaming buffer. That buffer is flushed to the assembler only to produce the final response; token fragments are not written as separate objects. If a client cancels mid-stream, nothing is written except whatever assembled final response existed at cancellation time (if any).

- KV cache/session: KV cache entries are stored in ephemeral local disk or node memory depending on the runtime and are not included in backup snapshots. They are evicted per LRU and TTL policies and are not queryable via the metadata index.

- Deletion flow & evidence: 
  * Tombstone step: customer-initiated deletes and system purges mark artifact ids as tombstoned in the metadata DB immediately.
  * Purge step: an asynchronous purge job removes object-store blobs and updates indices. Typical window: tombstone -> object deletion completes within 72 hours under normal ops.
  * Backups: we take daily encrypted backups; deleted artifacts in backups are retained for an additional 30 days on encrypted snapshots. We can provide a deletion certificate that includes: artifact ids, tombstone timestamp, purge completion timestamp, and the blob checksums removed.

- Edge cases (important): 
  * If a request was routed to a Dedicated/Private deployment with customer-managed object store, deletion responsibilities and timelines follow the customer environment (we provide hooks/runbooks).
  * For synchronous transcripts exported to third-party integrations (S3, Data Warehouse), customers control deletion in those downstream locations. We can include explicit delete webhooks to notify and optionally trigger downstream erasure.

- Residency specifics: 
  * Hosted: routing uses region affinity; we store artifacts in the region where the request was served. We do not automatically replicate user request artifacts across regions.
  * Dedicated/Private: storage region is customer-configurable; for strict EU-only obligations we recommend Private with customer VPC + KMS.

Attachments: I attached a short internal deletion runbook and an excerpted SOC2 evidence stub to illustrate the certificate format. If FinBridge needs an itemized checklist for procurement (e.g., DPA language, backup retention clause), I can prepare that as a one-pager.

Kimberly Park
Sr. Security & Compliance Engineer, Redwood Inference
kimberly@redwood.com
Attachments: redwood-deletion-runbook.pdf, soc2-evidence-stub.pdf
